extracted.intended_audience: covered entities (health programs and activities), health plans/issuers, health care providers, legal/compliance staff, and OCR/regulatory staff
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the compliance requirements, procedural standards, and cost/benefit assessment metrics in the HHS final rule implementing Section 1557 (nondiscrimination in health programs/activities). Focuses on notices, training, documentation, decision support tools, exemption requests, and coverage nondiscrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Nondiscrimination and Notice of Availability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires the 266,297 covered entities to provide a Notice of Nondiscrimination to participants, enrollees, and beneficiaries of its health program or activity, and members of the public. It also requires covered entities to provide a Notice of Availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types of notices are required (1) on an annual basis; (2) upon request; (3) at a conspicuous location on the covered entity's health program or activity website; and (4) in clear and prominent physical locations where the health program or activity interacts with the public. The approach provides a narrower set of situations than the 2016 Rule but retains these core placement/frequency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications requiring Notice of Availability (enumerated list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice of Availability is required in specified electronic and written communications related to the covered entity's health programs and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated communications: (1) notice of nondiscrimination required by final §92.10; (2) notice of privacy practices required by 45 CFR 164.520; (3) application and intake forms; (4) notices of denial or termination of benefits or services, including Explanations of Benefits (EOBs) and notices of appeal and grievance rights; (5) communications related to an individual's rights, eligibility benefits, or services that require or request a response from a beneficiary; (6) communications related to a public health emergency; (7) consent forms and instructions related to medical procedures or operations, medical power of attorney, or living will (option to bundle documents and provide one notice); (8) discharge papers; (9) communications related to the cost and payment of care (including good faith estimates and medical billing and collections materials); (10) complaint forms; and (11) patient and member handbooks. The Department increased the count of communications by 10% to cover additional cost/payment communications not in the Proposed Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out for Notice of Availability on EOBs
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule at §92.11(d) permits covered entities to provide individuals with the option to opt out of receiving the Notice of Availability on an annual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This opt-out option reduces cost and burden associated with including the Notice of Availability on EOBs. The Department notes that EOBs are often an individual's first and sometimes only notice of denial/termination, so the requirement is considered essential despite the opt-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice cost-estimation methodology and electronic-adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA adopts per-unit print-and-fold cost estimates and adjusts for electronic delivery to estimate aggregate costs of notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary per-unit print/fold cost: midpoint estimate $0.05 (2010 dollars); sensitivity range $0.03–$0.07. Adjusted to 2022 dollars using the Implicit Price Deflator yields a primary per-unit estimate ≈ $0.067 and a full range ≈ $0.045–$0.37. Following the 2020 RIA approach, the aggregate figure is adjusted downward by 50% to account for lower cost of electronic communications, using respondents' reported share using digital contact methods. Combining counts and per-unit costs produces an adjusted annual primary estimate of $46.6 million (range $28.6M–$261.4M). The RIA also reports low/high sensitivity scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and record-retention requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires covered entities to contemporaneously document activities performed under the rule (e.g., employees' completion of required training) and to retain certain records, including records related to grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grievance records must be stored for no less than three (3) years. Cost-model assumptions: one employee per covered entity with more than 15 employees (63,950 entities) spending 10 hours annually to store complaints/records; assumed occupation is administrative/clerical support with mean hourly wage $19.02 doubled to account for overhead/indirect costs. Training documentation costs modeled as: 0.25 hours to create sign-up forms in first year and 1 hour to collect/store attendance forms in first and subsequent years, with same wage assumptions. Resulting cost estimates: $24.3M annually for grievance retention; $12.6M first year and $10.1M subsequent years for documenting training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements, scope, and compliance timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule establishes training requirements (final §92.9) and a compliance timeline: covered entities must comply with the §92.9 Training requirements by no later than 300 days of the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIA assumes expanded training coverage under the final rule (from 50% baseline to 75% of employees receiving training, i.e., 25% incremental). It models initial and ongoing training costs (including annual refresher training and training for new employees). OCR assumes 91 investigators (equivalent to GS-12 Step 1) will receive an 8-hour one-time training in the first year. The RIA also assumes covered entities may require 1 hour of training in response to an OCR investigation; frequency modeled using 60 section-1557 investigations closed in 2023 as baseline. Training must be documented contemporaneously (see documentation requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to revise policies and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department anticipates that all covered entities (~266,297) will revise their policies and procedures under the final rule, with approximately half requiring more extensive revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling assumptions: for more extensive revisions, 4 total hours per entity (3 hours by a mid-level manager [SOC 43-1011], 1 hour by executive staff [SOC 11-1021]); for less extensive revisions, 2 total hours (1 mid-level manager, 1 executive). Adjusted hourly wages (including fringe/indirect costs) yield per-entity costs of $307.08 (extensive) or $181.12 (less extensive). For 133,149 entities of each type, total estimated cost ≈ $65.0M. The RIA also assumes that revisions following OCR investigations will occur in response to half of investigations and uses the same per-entity cost structure to estimate annual corrective revision costs (~$7,323 modeled). The RIA notes uncertainty due to wide variation of entity types/sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision support tool nondiscrimination and mitigation requirement (§92.210)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 92.210 sets a minimum requirement for each covered entity to make reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination resulting from the covered entity's use of a decision support tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR models review time: all covered entities (266,297) take 1 hour to review decision support tools in year 1 and 0.5 hours in years 2–5 (assumes half-hour 1557 coordinator and half-hour Management Analyst or equivalent). Adjusted hourly wages give per-entity review cost $69.34 year 1 and $34.67 in subsequent years, producing aggregate costs of $18,465,034 in year 1 and $9,232,517 annually in years 2–5. If review finds no evidence of discriminatory outputs, no further action/cost; if discriminatory risk identified, entities must take reasonable mitigation steps. Mitigation options include: notifying the third-party vendor, altering usage/policies to account for bias, switching products if feasible, updating internally-developed tools, or other reasonable mitigation measures. OCR did not quantify costs of mitigation due to data limitations and variability; larger entities likely to have higher mitigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance-of-exemption request process and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities may submit requests for assurance of an exemption based on Federal conscience or religious freedom laws; the RIA models the time and cost burden associated with submitting such exemption assurance requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled process: two employees spending two hours each to assess need; one employee spending three hours writing and submitting the request. Assumed occupations: legal personnel (lawyers/legal assistants) with mean hourly wage $70.55 doubled for overhead; estimated cost per exemption request ≈ $987.70. OCR's processing cost model: single lawyer-equivalent employee spending 3 hours (wage doubled) to review each request; cost per review computed accordingly. OCR revised its estimate of number of requests to 6,019 in year 1 (707 religious hospitals + 2% of other covered entities), producing modeled totals: ~$5.94M cost to covered entities and ~$2.55M cost to OCR for review, total ~$8.49M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage nondiscrimination requirement (gender-affirming care) and applicability timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not mandate provision or coverage of specific services (including gender-affirming care), but requires that to the extent a covered entity provides coverage for a particular health service, it must provide that service to all individuals in a neutral, nondiscriminatory manner consistent with the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIA assesses potential incremental costs of coverage for gender-affirming care and concludes likely small/immaterial impacts based on cited studies and low utilization rates among transgender individuals. The RIA presents upper-bound, lower-bound, and primary estimates: upper-bound $546M annually (using 0.012% incremental cost applied to total health expenditures), lower-bound $0 (fully offset by reductions in other spending), and a primary estimate that after adjustments yields ≈ $138M per year starting in year 2 (2025). The RIA also notes delayed applicability dates for coverage provisions (§92.207(b)(1)–(6))—effective first day of first plan year beginning on or after January 1, 2025—so no coverage cost in 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on benefit quantification and attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA documents important challenges and limitations in quantifying and monetizing benefits arising from the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key limitations: attribution issues (benefits may overlap with existing civil rights regulation, ACA, State law, or institutional policies); lack of quantitative linkage between nondiscrimination policies and health outcomes (e.g., reduced refusals, reductions in morbidity/mortality); inability to estimate magnitude of discriminatory events attributable to the rule; inability to monetize improvements such as reductions in suicidal ideation, substance use, or mental health improvements. The RIA therefore discusses anticipated but unquantified benefits (reduced enforcement actions, benefits from grievance procedures, reduced language barriers, and benefits from decision support tool nondiscrimination) and notes that these are not captured in the monetary benefit analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance-timeline flexibility (comparison to Proposed Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department considered and adopted a revised compliance timeline that allows additional time for covered entities to comply with certain procedural requirements compared to the Proposed Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: covered entities must comply with §92.9 Training by no later than 300 days after the effective date (postponing some costs). The RIA notes that because impacts are reported on an annual basis, the revised timeline does not change the annual quantified cost estimates, though it postpones when covered entities incur certain costs.
